title: IAM Least-Privilege Policies & Keyless OIDC Identity
summary: Master IAM explicit Deny precedence, Instance Profiles, short-lived STS tokens, and GitHub Actions OIDC keyless authentication.
learningObjectives: Audit and tighten wildcard IAM policies down to scoped resources and actions
Eliminate static long-lived secret access keys using temporary IAM roles and OIDC federation
prerequisiteConcepts: Understanding of cloud compute and object storage

sections.heading: 1. IAM Policy Evaluation & Role Delegation
sections.content:
In Cloud IAM, requests follow strict deterministic evaluation: Explicit Deny ALWAYS overrides Allow, any missing Allow defaults to Implicit Deny, and an action succeeds ONLY when explicitly allowed with zero matching Denies.

Production systems NEVER embed static `AKIA...` access key pairs in environment variables on servers or CI pipelines. Instead, workloads attach IAM Roles (issuing rotating temporary short-lived STS credentials automatically) or federate via OpenID Connect (OIDC) tokens from GitHub Actions claiming exact repo/branch identity.

codeExamples.code:
GitHub Actions Workflow --(Signed OIDC JWT)--> Cloud STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
                                                      | (Verifies repo + main branch claim)
                                                      v
                                            Temporary 15m Scoped Role Token (Zero static keys!)
codeExamples.explanation: OIDC federation eliminates exposed long-lived secrets in Git repositories and CI settings entirely.

keyPoints: An Explicit Deny rule beats any Allow rule even if attached to an admin.
Use Condition keys (`aws:SecureTransport`, `aws:SourceVpc`) to lock down API transport and network origin.
commonMistakes: Assigning `Action: "*"` and `Resource: "*"` temporarily during development and deploying it straight to production.

sections.heading: 2. Least-Privilege Policy Refactored Example
sections.content: Compare a dangerous wildcard configuration against a production least-privilege policy permitting strictly `s3:GetObject` over one bucket prefix while explicitly denying object deletion and insecure plaintext HTTP.

codeExamples.explanation: Scoping both Action list and exact bucket ARN prevents lateral access across other buckets even if application dependencies are compromised.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Valid least-privilege IAM policy allowing strictly scoped reads and explicitly blocking destruction

keyPoints: Audit Service Control Policies (SCPs) at organization level as unbreakable guardrails across accounts.
commonMistakes: Granting read access on `arn:aws:s3:::*` instead of naming exact buckets.

exercises.title: Tighten Over-Privileged CI Deployment IAM Policy
exercises.objective: Eliminate wildcard permissions while preserving deploy functionality.
exercises.description: Refactor a wildcard policy (`Effect: Allow, Action: *, Resource: *`) down to allowing ONLY uploading objects to `careertwin-web-dist` and enforcing TLS.
instructions: Replace `Action: '*'` with exact object upload action (`s3:PutObject`).
hints: Explicit Deny + `aws:SecureTransport: false` blocks HTTP plaintext traffic permanently.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Explicit scoped allow plus TLS enforcement limits CI capabilities purely to secure deployment uploads.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: If a developer belongs to Group A allowing `s3:DeleteBucket` and also has an explicit policy statement denying `s3:DeleteBucket`, what happens when they call DeleteBucket?

options.text: AccessDenied: Explicit Deny always overrides any Allow statement
Allowed because Group permissions beat user permissions
The call succeeds only from CLI

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Explicit Deny takes absolute precedence across all policy evaluation stages.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Why is OIDC federation preferable to saving long-lived static cloud access keys in GitHub Actions secrets?

options.text: Temporary STS tokens auto-expire quickly and are cryptographically bound to specific repositories/branches with zero static keys to leak
Static keys cannot upload files larger than 1MB
GitHub deletes static secrets after 1 hour

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Keyless federation eliminates credential rotation headaches and long-term secret leakage risks.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: In an IAM policy condition blocking unencrypted S3 traffic, which condition checks HTTPS?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Denying requests whenever `aws:SecureTransport` evaluates to false ensures encrypted TLS calls only.

recap: You mastered deterministic IAM evaluation, least-privilege JSON authoring, and keyless OIDC CI authentication.
